title: Linear approximation at an operating point

sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A smooth curve, with room for a tangent at one point.
sections.body_md: A smooth function is hard to carry through a design and easy to replace near one point. Pick that point first. Read the function there, and read the derivative there. The linear approximation is the value plus the derivative times the step away from the point. Nothing in the formula looks at the function at the far end of the step.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md: For a scalar function, \[ f(a) + f'(a)\,(x - a). \] The step is \(x - a\). The derivative is \(f'(a)\), not \(f'(x)\). If \(f\) is smooth, the error satisfies \[ f(x) - \big(f(a) + f'(a)\,(x - a)\big) = o(|x - a|) \] as the step shrinks. The error goes to zero faster than the step, which is why a small step is trustworthy and a large step is not. The same sentence in several variables uses the gradient in place of \(f'(a)\), still evaluated at the chosen point.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(g(z) = z^2\) at \(z = 7\), and take a step of \(0.3\). The value is \(49\). The derivative \(2z\) equals \(14\) at this point, so the predicted change is \(14 \cdot 0.3 = 4.2\) and the approximation is \(53.2\). The true value at \(7.3\) is \(53.29\). The miss is \(0.09\), much smaller than the step \(0.3\). The slope at \(7.3\) would be a different expansion. The ratio \(49/7 = 7\) is the value divided by the coordinate, not the slope that multiplies the step.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: - Evaluating the derivative at the new point. The slope in the formula is the slope at the chosen point. - Reporting the slope and forgetting to add the value. The approximation is a value plus a change. - Using the ratio of the value to the coordinate as if it were the derivative. Those agree only for a line through the origin. - Treating a large step as if the higher-order error were still negligible. The formula does not become exact just because it was written down.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: When the function is stored charge versus voltage, the slope is a small-signal capacitance. When the function is a rate that depends on a state and an input, the same replacement at a resting condition becomes two partial derivatives. When a second derivative is available, a later expansion adds that term on top of this linear model. Each of those skills starts from the value and the first derivative already built here.
